name: boston baked beans
instructions:
Traditional New England slow-baked bean dish — white beans, pork, molasses, and dijon mustard baked low and slow for hours until the beans absorb the sweet-smoky sauce. Canonical version below; adjust to taste on future cooks.

=== INGREDIENTS ===

- 1 lb dried WHITE BEANS (great northern or similar; small beans traditional)
- 1/2 lb PORK — pork shoulder cubed, pork belly cubed, OR thick-cut bacon in large pieces. Any of the three works.
- 1 yellow onion, coarsely chopped or halved
- 1/2 cup MOLASSES
- OPTIONAL: 1/4 to 1/3 cup brown sugar (secondary — molasses carries the sweetness on its own; brown sugar is a boost when you want more)
- 2 tbsp DIJON MUSTARD
- 1 tsp salt (adjust based on the pork's saltiness)
- 1/2 tsp black pepper
- water (enough to just cover the beans in the pot)
- OPTIONAL: 1-2 tbsp apple cider vinegar (finish); a splash of ketchup or worcestershire for depth

=== PROCEDURE ===

1. SOAK THE BEANS overnight in cold water (or use a quick-soak: cover with water, boil 2 min, off heat 1 hour). Drain.
2. PARBOIL: cover soaked beans with fresh water, bring to a simmer, cook ~10-15 min until the skins start to curl when you blow on a spoonful. Drain, reserve the liquid.
3. BUILD THE POT: in a bean pot or Dutch oven, layer the pork in the bottom, then the onion, then the beans on top. In a separate bowl whisk molasses + brown sugar + dijon mustard + salt + pepper with some of the reserved bean liquid. Pour over the beans. Add enough additional water (or reserved liquid) to just cover the beans.
4. BAKE COVERED at 275-300°F for 4-6 hours. Check every hour and add water if the beans start to dry out — they should stay just barely covered throughout the bake.
5. UNCOVER for the last 30-60 min to let the top develop color and the sauce thicken.
6. Taste and adjust. A splash of apple cider vinegar at the end can lift the sweetness if it reads too flat.
notes:
=== SLOW AND LOW IS THE WHOLE TECHNIQUE ===

Boston baked beans are defined by the long slow bake — 4-6 hours at 275-300°F is the target range. This is what gives the beans time to fully absorb the molasses-and-mustard sauce and develop the deep sweet-smoky character. Shortcuts (higher heat, shorter bake) don't produce the same result — you end up with beans in sauce rather than beans OF sauce.

=== MOLASSES IS LOAD-BEARING ===

The molasses is what makes boston baked beans distinctively BOSTON. Its bitter-sweet, slightly mineral character is the signature — swapping in pure brown sugar or maple syrup produces a sweeter, less complex dish. Molasses non-optional. Blackstrap is too bitter; use regular unsulphured molasses.

=== PORK — POCK SHOULDER, PORK BELLY, OR BACON — ALL WORK ===

Any of the three works structurally. Traditional New England uses salt pork; pork belly or thick-cut bacon are practical modern substitutes; pork shoulder cubed gives you a leaner braised-meat component. Bacon lends more smoke; belly/shoulder give more meat texture. Pick based on what's available.

ADD LARD IF YOUR PORK IS TOO LEAN (SECONDARY): if you're using a lean cut of pork (shoulder cubed, or lean bacon) and the pot is coming out dry, a spoonful of lard rendered in with the beans adds the fat depth the leaner cut isn't providing on its own. Skip if using pork belly or fatty bacon.

=== DIJON OVER DRY MUSTARD ===

Canonical recipes often call for dry mustard powder; dijon works well here as a substitute (and is what I keep on hand). The prepared mustard contributes similar mustard depth plus a small vinegar hit that helps balance the molasses sweetness.

=== WHITE BEANS — GREAT NORTHERN OR SIMILAR ===

Small white beans traditional (navy beans are the classical pick; great northern also works). Use dried and soak overnight — canned white beans work in a pinch but lose the sauce-absorption benefit that dried beans deliver during the long bake.

=== BAKE COVERED, UNCOVER TO FINISH ===

Covered for the bulk of the bake keeps the beans moist and lets the sauce integrate. Uncover for the last 30-60 min so the top develops color and the sauce thickens down. Both stages matter.

=== ACID FINISH (OPTIONAL) ===

A splash of apple cider vinegar at the end can lift the dish if the sweetness reads too heavy. Not classical; a modern adjustment. Skip if the balance already feels right.

=== SIBLING RECIPES ===

- italian-tomato-white-beans + italian-no-tomato-white-beans: same white-bean base, different flavor register (italian herbs + tomato vs boston molasses + pork).
- mexican-black-beans: another slow-cooked bean dish; different bean, different flavor axis, but similar low-and-slow philosophy.
- lemony-shrimp-and-bean-stew: another white-bean dish; brothy/lemony vs sweet/smoky.
